motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the Policies and Procedures Manual Regarding Continuing Education Reimbursement and Paydays. This item was discussed after item 14.B. Human Resource Manager Angela Valenzuela explained the City currently reimburses employees up to $1,500 for continuing education. Generally, three to four employees use the benefits each year. To be in line with other municipal reimbursement programs, staff proposes to raise the reimbursement up to $2,500 per year per employee, or up to 75% of the cost. The funding supports job-specific certification programs or department head-approved college courses related to the employee’s job duties. The second change to the manual is to change the payday from Thursday to Friday to accurately reflect current procedures. Councilmembers Clark and Love expressed their support of the program as a mutual benefit to and investment in the City and City employees.
motions.motion: Councilmember Love moved to approve a resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, amending the Policies and Procedures Manual regarding continuing education reimbursement and paydays. Councilmember Burnham seconded the motion. Those voting aye: Donna Burnham, Melissa Clark, Colby Curtis, and Carolyn Love. The motion passed with a unanimous vote.

motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Adopting Firework Restrictions for 2021. This item was discussed prior to item 12.A. Mayor Westmoreland stated fire restrictions in Salt Lake County were discussed during a Unified Fire Service Area meeting earlier in the day. They struck a balance between enforcement and safety. Residents in some areas of the City have requested additional restrictions to the Fireworks Restriction Map. The State and Federal government have restricted fireworks and open fires on all public lands. He believes it would be wise for the City to impose similar restrictions following the State and Federal guidelines in consideration of combustible materials, drought conditions, high temperatures, and winds. Councilmember Clark said other cities have decided to provide professional firework displays as an alternative to family and neighborhood fireworks. Mayor Westmoreland said that the City wants to encourage safely celebrating with alternative activities during the 4th of July and 24th of July. Councilmember Curtis expressed reluctance to imposing restrictions that impact law-abiding citizens and are ignored by others. He is in favor of approving the more restrictive map but is hesitant to impose a City-wide fireworks ban. Sergeant B.J. Eccles agreed with the likelihood that some citizens will light fireworks despite restrictions; however, the majority will comply. He applauded residents that follow regulations. If there are fireworks, there will be fires. He noted enforcement of firework restrictions in addition to regular duties becomes cumbersome, but the Sheriff’s Office will strive to enforce the Council’s directives. Councilmember Burnham explained, in light of her statements during work session, that she dislikes taking liberties away from people; nevertheless, she has the right to drink water. One major fire would have a disastrous impact on the City’s water supply. Her role and responsibilities as a member of the City Council require her to consider impacts. Banning fireworks City-wide simplifies and clarifies the restrictions. She supports the idea of an alternate celebration activity to commemorate the importance of the holidays. Her advocacy for restrictions is due to drought and water supply considerations. Councilmember Curtis clarified he understands the gravity of the concerns. As State Code prohibits the banning of a specific type of firework, should the Council determine to implement a City-wide firework restriction, it must prohibit all fireworks. Councilmember Love said that it is a difficult decision. In her opinion, lighting fireworks will result in fires. She agrees that it is important to reserve water for drinking rather than fighting fires; water needs are more vital than lighting fireworks. Discussion ensued regarding the amount of water required to suppress a fire depending upon the size and severity of a fire and threat to life and property. Councilmember Clark echoed the concerns of her fellow Councilmembers to balance the celebration of liberty with protecting the rights surrounding health, safety, welfare, and property, and preserving the water supply. She stated an alternate City celebratory activity would be far less expensive than putting out a fire. United Fire Authority Battalion Chief Embret Fossum explained the City is in the middle of a red flag warning that includes high winds, heat and low humidity. This means the City faces a conflagration anytime that a fire sparks. The combination of the drought and heat during a red flag warning increases the likelihood of a severe fire. During similar conditions last year in Oregon, a fire burned through over 4,000 homes and caused major loss of life. Record-breaking temperatures this early in the year become problematic and the combination of factors places the City in a dire situation. He said it falls to the elected officials to determine restrictions for fireworks and open fires. Type One fires are the largest designation. Type Two fires are large and require teams of 500 to 2,000 firefighters. Already this year within the State of Utah, four type two teams have been assembled which was previously unprecedented this early in a fire season. Fireworks are an element that can be mitigated. Although enforcement falls to the Sheriff’s department, he feels that a full ban is easier to enforce. Councilmember Gray left the meeting at 8:15 p.m. due to technical difficulties. Councilmember Love inquired if a restriction on open fires could be included in the motion. Mayor Westmoreland and Ms. Kofoed clarified the State ban is for open fires on State lands and could be applied to public lands within City limits. The City Council may exclude fit pits on private land within landscaped areas. Councilmember Curtis said after considerations, he is willing to stand with Councilmembers on a decision even though it might not be popular with some residents. Discussion ensued regarding the complexities of the problem and the responsibility of the Council to mitigate the potential for a devastating fire due to current circumstances and the information provided.
motions.motion: Councilmember Burnham moved to approve a resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, adopting a fireworks ban prohibiting fireworks during the July 4th and July 24th, 2021 holiday celebration and restricting open flame fires in undeveloped land until August 31, 2021. Councilmember Curtis seconded the motion. Those voting aye: Donna Burnham, Melissa Clark, Colby Curtis, and Carolyn Love. The motion passed with a unanimous vote.

Those voting aye: Donna Burnham, Melissa Clark, Colby Curtis, and Carolyn Love. The motion passed with a unanimous vote. 14.C. ORDINANCE/PUBLIC HEARING – An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Adopting an Impact Fee Enactment for a Public Safety Impact Fee; Providing for the Calculation and Collection of Such Fees; Providing for Appeal, Accounting, and Severability of the Same and Other Related Matters. Lewis Young Robertson and Burningham Vice President Fred Philpot presented the item and explained the impact fee process. The Impact Facility Plan and Impact Fee Analysis process considered the service area and demand, level of service (LOS), existing facilities and buy-in, future facilities, financing, and proportionate share analysis. The police proportionate share analysis determined a total impact fee cost of $11,109,356 and an $820,971 cost to impact fee. The proposed police impact fee schedule based upon a $66 cost per call and 0.633 residential calls per unit and 2.190 non-residential calls per unit, per 1,000 square feet, resulted in a proposed impact fee of $42 for residential and $145 for non-residential units. Impact fees for non-standard developments will be calculated separately based upon the $66 cost per call and the number of calls per calculation per unit for the non-standard use type. The next steps include holding the public hearing noticed for this meeting; the Council adopting, modifying, or rejecting the proposed impact fees; and a 90-day wait period prior to implementing an approved impact fee increase. Mr. Philpot explained that the proposed $42 residential impact is lower than the typical $150 up to $350 range found in other communities. The lower impact fee is due to the low square footage LOS. The City can reevaluate the LOS after constructing new facilities and adjust the impact fee

motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving a Development Agreement between Eagle Mountain City, Utah and Curleybird, LLC. Economic Development Director Aaron Sanborn presented the item. The 320 acres of undeveloped land is located adjacent to the Facebook site on two separate parcels within the Regional Technology and Industry Overlay zone. The proposal is for an enterprise-level data center with an initial investment of approximately $600,000,000 and about 3,000 square feet of building space in the initial construction. The project has received previous approval from the Eagle Mountain Redevelopment Agency (RDA) Board for the creation of a community reinvestment area and associated tax-increment financing. Interlocal agreements have been approved by the RDA board and the individual taxing entities. The development agreement defines the rights and obligations of Curleybird LLC and the City specific to a multi-year, large-scale data center project. If a company does not qualify for a State exemption on the Municipal Energy Tax (MET), the company is eligible for reimbursement of the MET, up to 80%, if using renewable energy sources. For comparison, Facebook receives a 100% reimbursement. Large investment in infrastructure will occur in several phases to be bid and built by the City and reimbursed by the company. Additionally, the City may request up to $3,000,000 in reimbursement for damage and wear to roads due to the project. The company is required to pay impact fees according to City policies. The company may not prepay impact fees and will be charged the impact fee rates at the time of building permit application. The company may receive impact fee credits according to City policies. The term of the contract is 40 years from the effective date. The contract will be renegotiated if the roadway improvements have not commenced within five years, if the plan is not submitted for the initial phase within seven years, or if construction has not commenced within ten years. Councilmember Love asked if the agreement had a contingency clause to address construction delays. City Attorney Jeremy Cook said the company is responsible for reimbursing any construction or improvements that benefit their project within the period specified and pre- and post-periods. Difficulties in structuring the agreement arose due to the uncertainty regarding the construction period, particularly regarding the water infrastructure, and the payment schedule was adapted accordingly. He requested the Council grant staff the authority to make adjustments to the agreements including language regarding lowering the liability cap and wording clarifications to remove ambiguity. Mr. Sanborn explained that Exhibit D(1) Project Freemont Road Improvements was referenced in the agreement but excluded from the packet materials and will be included in the agreement.
motions.motion: Councilmember Curtis moved to approve a resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, approving a development agreement between Eagle Mountain City, Utah, and Curleybird, LLC including Exhibit D(1) Project Freemont Road Improvements and permitting staff to make adjustments to the liability cap and non-substantive wording amendments. Councilmember Clark seconded the motion. Those voting aye: Donna Burnham, Melissa Clark, Colby Curtis, and Carolyn Love. The motion passed with a unanimous vote.

motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving a Water and Sewer Agreement between Eagle Mountain City, Utah and Curleybird, LLC. Mr. Sanborn presented the item. The Water and Sewer Agreement defines the rights and obligations of Curleybird LLC and the City, specific to a multi-year, large-scale data center project. The City will reserve 1,000 acre-feet of water initially that expires if certain milestones are not met. The company has the option of refusal on an additional 2,000 acre-feet of water and 30 days to secure water if the City’s remaining capacity under current agreements drops to 3,000 acre-feet. The company will pay current prices for shares and water rates. An annual report will show actual water needs and the company will purchase enough water to meet demands. The City may use secondary water from the company for a water reuse system that can be used for other industrial customers, open space, and potentially for resident use in the future. Some businesses have expressed interest in reusing the secondary water from the data centers to reduce their water use impact. Mr. Cook stated that the liability cap changes also impact this agreement and should be included in the motion.
motions.motion: Councilmember Curtis moved to approve a resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, approving a water and sewer agreement between Eagle Mountain City, Utah and Curleybird, LLC permitting staff to make adjustments to the liability cap and non-substantive wording amendments. Councilmember Clark seconded the motion. Those voting aye: Donna Burnham, Melissa Clark, Colby Curtis, and Carolyn Love. The motion passed with a unanimous vote.
